state.case_summary:
A 58-year-old woman presented to the rheumatology clinic with a 2-month history of fatigue, weakness, polyarthritis, and joint swelling. Nine months earlier, she had been diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary hypertension after a 3-year history of progressive dyspnea (now NYHA class IV) and orthopnea, without cough or sputum, accompanied by low-grade fever and night sweats. Echocardiography at that time showed a pulmonary arterial systolic pressure (PASP) of 80 mm Hg, a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, mild mitral regurgitation, and moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation. Chest CT revealed alveolar infiltrates in the posterior segment of the left basal lobe and multiple 6–8 mm peripheral lung nodules. Vital signs were normal, and pulmonary function testing was within normal limits.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 45 mm/h, an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:320, and an anti-centromere antibody level of 94.8 AU/ml. Tests for anti–Scl-70, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and rheumatoid arthritis were negative.

On examination, there was effusion of the right second, third, and fourth metacarpophalangeal joints; right second and third proximal interphalangeal joints; left second, third, and fourth metacarpophalangeal joints; and left fourth and fifth proximal interphalangeal joints. Raynaud’s phenomenon was elicited by cold‐water immersion of the hands. Chest auscultation revealed coarse crackles. Repeat echocardiography showed a PASP of 55 mm Hg after treatment, and ECG demonstrated sinus bradycardia with P pulmonale and biphasic P waves.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. systemic sclerosis sine scleroderma
B. Idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension was the initial diagnosis because of progressive dyspnea and an elevated PASP
C. Rheumatoid arthritis was considered given the polyarthritis and joint effusions but was excluded because “rheumatoid
D. Limited or diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis was considered but excluded on the basis of no skin changes
E. Systemic sclerosis sine scleroderma was established when internal organ involvement, Raynaud’s phenomenon, positive anti
F. None
